nutshell: Multiple pedestrian trajectory forecasting is normally done as a two-stage pipeline (detect+track, then forecast), which gets slower as more people appear in a scene. S2F2 instead does detection, Re-ID, and forecasting in one single-stage network built on FairMOT, predicting future optical flow maps (via a GRU-based decoder) that are used to warp current detections forward into future bounding boxes, keeping inference cost constant regardless of pedestrian count.
contributions: A single-stage architecture sharing one backbone/feature extractor across detection, Re-ID, and forecasting, replacing the two-stage detect-then-forecast paradigm.

A 'future flow decoder' (ConvGRU-based) trained with a supervised center-displacement loss plus an unsupervised SSIM warping loss, predicting n future optical flow maps all referenced back to the same starting frame (rather than chaining frame-to-frame) specifically to avoid error accumulation.

A forecasting-refinement modification to FairMOT's tracking/association step that lowers the detection-confidence threshold for boxes near a forecasted future location, to recover low-confidence (e.g. occluded) detections.
Demonstrates near-constant forecasting latency (~13.8ms) regardless of pedestrian density, versus the two-stage STED baseline whose inference time grows with the number of people in the scene.
deficiencies: The paper builds its own benchmark (StaticMOT) specifically excluding camera ego-motion sequences, and never evaluates on the ego-motion sequences it explicitly calls out as 'hard cases' - so the comparison sidesteps exactly the harder condition (moving-camera video) that would stress-test the approach.

The forecasting gains over the training-free Constant-Velocity baseline are real but modest (ADE 12.275 vs 14.481, ~15% relative) given the added complexity of a full joint detection+Re-ID+forecasting network versus a simple 3-frame velocity heuristic.

Table 4 shows the tracking accuracy gain over the underlying FairMOT baseline it's built on is very small (MOTA 70.0 vs 69.8 on MOT17 test) and ID switches actually get worse (4590 vs 3996) - attributed in the text to 'slight overfitting' with no further investigation or mitigation.

All ablations (Tables 5 and 6) report single-run numbers with margins often under 1 MOTA point (e.g. 67.7 vs 67.6), with no variance or repeated-seed reporting to indicate whether the design choices being validated (own tracker vs. ByteTrack, refinement vs. none) are meaningfully better than noise.
notable: The future flow decoder deliberately anchors every predicted flow map back to the same starting frame I_t (so f_{t+n} is flow from I_t to I_{t+n} directly, not chained through I_{t+n-1}) specifically to avoid compounding warping errors across timesteps - a reusable pattern for other multi-step forecast-via-warping designs. The 'Ours+PastDetach' ablation (Table 5) is also a useful negative result: adding an auxiliary past-flow-prediction task with a fully detached gradient path helps detection accuracy but makes forecasting worse than the non-detached 'Ours+Past' variant, suggesting shared-gradient multi-task features generalize better here than cleanly separated ones.
